source.title: Demystifying Training-Time Augmentation for Data-Constrained Language Model Pretraining
source.authors: Michael Chen; Xi-Kun Zhang; Fan Bai; Zheng-Ding Hu; Zhen D. Wang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss during repeated-data training and reports that it rises after an early minimum, explicitly describing this as a regime where a cited repeated-data scaling law does not model the observed behavior. It also compares validation loss with downstream accuracy.
record.gate_note: The study tests one 150M-parameter model on one fixed 75M-token corpus; it does not fit parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling power laws or compare model sizes. Augmentation ablations are not recorded as scaling-law rows. Prior results mentioned in related work are cited-only and are not rows.
record.test_reason: One 150M model on a fixed 75M-token corpus. The baseline's held-out loss over 100 repeated epochs falls to a minimum at epoch 16 and then rises. The authors explicitly argue this regime breaks the Muennighoff et al. repeated-data law (V5). Table 4 relates post-decay validation loss to zero-shot accuracy across eight training configurations at one scale (V6). No power laws are fitted and no model or data size is varied, so the test is narrow.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that standard AR training on a highly data-constrained fixed corpus peaks at epoch 16 and then degrades, a regime they say Muennighoff et al.'s repeated-data law does not model. Training-time augmentations, especially low-rate random replacement + R2L + exponential offset, delay overfitting and lower minimum loss (4.015 to 3.805). They state that lower loss translates to better downstream accuracy in aggregate, while individual benchmarks at 150M are too noisy to rank methods.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates training-time augmentation for repeated-data pretraining; it does not reproduce the scaling-law measurement or compute-optimal fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Augmentation choice and configuration affect validation loss and downstream results; the paper reports interactions among noise rate, sequence reversal, and offset prediction. Downstream rankings differ from validation-loss rankings.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-time augmentations (random replacement, R2L, exponentially weighted offset prediction, and their combinations) delay the repeated-data overfitting point and lower minimum held-out loss, from 4.015 to as low as 3.805 (stable phase) and 3.792 (decay).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Objective-level data augmentation shifts the repeated-data loss curve (later and lower optimum) in data-constrained AR pretraining.

record.problems: Evidence on scaling behavior is limited to one model size, one corpus, and one highly data-constrained regime. The study does not fit power laws or test predictions across model sizes. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors also note that downstream scores are highly variable at 150M parameters.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; only the baseline repeated-data trajectory and the aggregate downstream-accuracy comparisons bear directly on the tested claim versions. Individual benchmark scores and augmentation loss-minimum ablations were not extracted as scaling-law results.

untested.parts: No sweep over parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit; data is deliberately the bottleneck.
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit to the epoch curve. Only one model and data size. No other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer.
No downstream trend across model scale. Only one 150M model, with variation induced by training-objective augmentations.
No comparison of exponents, parameter counting or fitting methods.

missing.what: Five of ten benchmarks (LAMBADA, BoolQ, RTE, CommonsenseQA, ARC-Easy/OpenBookQA, SciQ) were excluded as non-discriminative. Retained tasks were chosen partly for showing 'a plausible ordering relative to validation loss', which biases the V6 loss–accuracy comparison.
Per-benchmark scores in Table 4 often contradict the loss ordering (e.g., PIQA is highest for baseline-adjacent Rand 15% and lowest for low-loss combinations).

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily an augmentation-methods paper; its bearing on scaling laws is limited to one baseline trajectory and a fixed-scale loss–accuracy comparison. The V6 evidence is weak for three reasons: variation comes from objective changes rather than scale, no uncertainty is reported, and benchmark retention was partly conditioned on agreement with loss. R1 could also be read as a curve bending away from a power law (V7), but V7 concerns fitted laws across setups, so it is not linked.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over parameter count, training tokens, or compute under non-bottleneck conditions; no power-law fit.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameter count and token count.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
Tests repeated-data pretraining only in one model/data setting; does not fit a power law, test other modalities, or test fine-tuning or transfer.
Tests downstream accuracy against validation loss across augmentation configurations at one model scale, not downstream performance across model scales.
Does not compare fitted exponents, parameter-counting conventions, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: 150M-parameter Llama-based causal language model
rows.operation_detail: Measured held-out validation loss over repeated epochs on a fixed corpus.
rows.value: Minimum 4.015 at epoch 16; loss then increases monotonically for the remainder of training.
rows.note: The authors state that this active degradation is not modeled by the cited repeated-data scaling law, which describes positive but diminishing returns. This is a single setting and not a direct power-law fit.
rows.check: State holds only after epoch 16: loss falls to 4.015 at epoch 16, then rises monotonically, 'well above the single-epoch baseline'. Data is deliberately the bottleneck (about 40x below Chinchilla). The row bears on repeated-data laws (V5), not on V1.

relationships.condition: Standard AR training, 150M model, fixed 75M-token corpus (about 40x below Chinchilla), 100 epochs
relationships.reason: Loss bottoms at 4.015 at epoch 16 and then rises monotonically. Authors say Muennighoff's repeated-data law does not model this degradation regime (R1). Single setting, no fit.
relationships.display_finding: Loss reached 4.015 at epoch 16 and then increased monotonically, entering a degradation regime that the repeated-data law did not model.

relationships.condition: Baseline vs all augmented configurations, aggregate mean over five retained benchmarks
relationships.reason: Baseline has the highest loss (4.000) and the lowest mean accuracy (41.0%). All seven lower-loss configurations score higher (41.2–43.3%) (R2–R9). The retained benchmarks were partly chosen for plausible ordering with loss.
relationships.display_finding: The baseline had loss 4.000 and accuracy 41.0%, while all seven lower-loss configurations reached 41.2–43.3%; benchmark selection partly favored plausible loss ordering.

relationships.condition: Among the seven augmented configurations at fixed 150M scale
relationships.reason: Loss does not predict accuracy rank. Best loss 3.792 ranks second (R9); 3.870 ranks first (R5). Near-equal losses 3.910 and 3.909 give 42.5% vs 41.2% (R4, R7). Authors call the ordinal correlation weak.
relationships.display_finding: Loss 3.792 ranked second in accuracy behind 3.870, while nearly equal losses of 3.910 and 3.909 yielded 42.5% and 41.2% accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
